discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations persist without NDRs means rule-driven shorts are excluded

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Macro/hierarchical-block pin-escape analysis on the hotspot boundary
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: all violations ringing one macro or block pin array confirms pin-escape/channel planning as the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations distributed mid-row away from any pin array excludes pin-access and points back at wire resources

common_root_causes.cause: Macro pin channels / pin escapes not planned wide enough
PG straps or clock trunks consuming specific layers through the region
NDR overuse on many nets through one corridor
Local hierarchy-boundary placement imbalance invisible in the global utilization number
Forgotten padding/inflation or keepout settings from an earlier congestion fix

items.classic_trap: globally lowering utilization targets and re-placing the whole block when the real problem is one macro pin channel or one strap lane; engineers blame the router first and burn a full rerun before measuring where the wire resources actually went
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, pin access, self-aligned via restrictions, and coloring/multi-patterning rules can masquerade as congestion shorts where 28nm violations were plain spacing

items.symptom: Setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Bucket the failing paths by clock domain and path group, and by launch/capture clock-gating cell
first_checks.why_first: cheapest report, and it immediately splits 'one clock tree is late' from 'everything degraded uniformly'

first_checks.check: Compare actual clock insertion delay per sink against what the pre-CTS scenario assumed
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most common cause — latency that the pre-CTS budget never modeled — in one report

first_checks.check: Check clock-net transition/slew at endpoints against the CTS spec targets
first_checks.why_first: a degraded slew on one trunk explains a whole subtree of failures in a single glance

first_checks.check: Diff the analysis setup against the last clean run: uncertainty, derate/OCV mode, corner assignment
first_checks.why_first: if the analysis changed, the physical timing may not have — this rules out a whole class of phantom regressions cheaply

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-time with the real propagated clock but the pre-CTS latency assumptions (or subtract the measured mean insertion delay from the failing slack)
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if slack recovers by roughly the added latency, the failure is unbudgeted insertion delay, not path degradation
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if slack does not recover, pure latency is excluded and real data/clock-path delay degradation is confirmed

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Trace each failing capture clock back to the root and compare tree depth against its launch counterpart
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: failing paths sharing one deep CTS subtree or one late CG cell while launch trees are shallow confirms a gating/branch latency imbalance
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: launch and capture trees of similar depth exclude tree-imbalance and point at data-path or model changes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Toggle the derate/OCV mode off in an analysis-only run
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violations vanishing means the post-CTS derating/OCV change is the cause, not physical delay
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations persisting excludes analysis-mode change as the explanation

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Measure routed/estimated detour ratio on the failing nets against the congestion map
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: failing nets detouring in congested regions confirms congestion-induced delay
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: straight, uncongested failing nets exclude congestion and leave cell delay or clock structure

common_root_causes.cause: Clock insertion latency never budgeted pre-CTS
Latency imbalance across clock-gating cells or branches
Analysis setting drift (uncertainty, derate, corner) between scenarios
Congestion detours inflating data-path delay
CTS run on a stale sink list or with wrong excluded pins

items.classic_trap: blaming the CTS tool for 'creating' bad timing when CTS merely exposed an optimistic pre-CTS budget; teams then waste iterations re-balancing skew when the fix is re-budgeting latency, not more balancing
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, insertion delay runs to hundreds of picoseconds across many buffer stages, so latency budgeting is survival; at 28nm ideal-clock flows often survived to route

items.symptom: Hold (min-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Split violations into same-clock-domain short paths vs cross-clock paths, and functional vs scan-shift paths
first_checks.why_first: cheapest split and it rules out the largest mis-scoped work — cross-clock and shift-mode paths need entirely different handling

first_checks.check: For each failing pair, read launch-vs-capture clock arrival and find their common point in the clock tree
first_checks.why_first: directly separates 'skew of the built tree' from 'path is just too short' in one look

first_checks.check: Verify the hold corner: fast library, min derate, correct mode
first_checks.why_first: a wrong corner shows up as systematic negative hold everywhere, which is instantly distinguishable from localized pairs

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run hold analysis with ideal (zero-skew) clock network
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violations disappearing under ideal clocks confirms the built tree's skew as the driver
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations persisting under ideal clocks excludes skew and confirms genuinely short data paths needing hold buffers or model fixes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Overlay violation locations on the CTS insertion-delay gradient map
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violations clustered where a steep latency gradient runs (e.g., past a macro cluster edge) confirms skew-gradient as cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations uniformly scattered across die independent of the gradient excludes tree-structure causes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Set hold-mode clock uncertainty to zero in an analysis-only pass
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: a clean result with zero uncertainty means the pessimism was uncertainty margin and real hold is routine to fix
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: still-negative slack with zero uncertainty excludes pessimism as the story

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Restrict the scenario to scan-shift clocks only and re-report
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: the whole violation set appearing only under shift confirms scan-chain hold scope, not functional logic
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: functional-only violations exclude the scan-path explanation

common_root_causes.cause: Very short data paths between adjacent flops awaiting routine hold fixing
Excessive local skew between close flop pairs
Scan/shift-mode hold paths never included in the checked scenario
Cross-clock paths wrongly assumed synchronous and chased for skew
Wrong min-corner or missing min derate

items.classic_trap: panicking over expected pre-hold-fix negatives and burning days re-balancing CTS, when the standard flow inserts hold buffers post-route anyway — or worse, fixing hold in functional mode only and shipping a chip that fails scan-shift
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below per-stage delay is small, so hold margin dominates and hold fixing consumes far more buffer area; at 28nm hold was a lighter afterthought

items.symptom: IR-drop-induced timing failure

first_checks.check: Run static IR analysis and overlay droop on the failing-instance map
first_checks.why_first: one run answers the whole 'is it power at all' question and rules out a pure timing-model problem if maps don't correlate

first_checks.check: Audit PG strap and rail density plus via-array counts in the failing region against spec
first_checks.why_first: missing straps or starved via arrays are visible by inspection and are the most frequent physical cause

first_checks.check: Correlate failing region with high-activity hierarchies (clock-heavy, wide data-path banks toggling together)
first_checks.why_first: activity correlation separates dynamic droop from static network resistance before deeper dynamic simulation is spent

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Static IR vs dynamic (vector- or activity-aware) IR comparison on the same region
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: static clean but dynamic showing local droop during activity windows confirms dynamic di/dt droop
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: static IR already showing the same hotspots excludes a purely dynamic story and confirms network resistance

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run timing with per-instance IR-derived voltage derating applied only to the drooping instances
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if per-instance derating reproduces exactly the observed failing set and magnitudes, IR is confirmed as the timing mechanism
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if per-instance derating explains none or a different set, IR-induced timing is excluded for those paths

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Trial fix: add straps/via arrays (or supply bumps) only in the hotspot and re-run IR
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: droop collapsing locally confirms the localized network was the bottleneck
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: droop persisting after local reinforcement pushes the cause outward to supply pads, package, or uniform grid insufficiency

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Stagger the enable timing of the large clock-gated banks in the activity model and re-run dynamic IR
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: peak droop dropping when wake-ups are staggered confirms simultaneous switching as the driver
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: droop insensitive to staggering excludes simultaneity and points back at DC resistance

common_root_causes.cause: Insufficient strap density or gaps around macros in the PG network
Dynamic di/dt underestimated; too little decoupling near the load
Starved via arrays at strap/rail junctions
Supply pad/bump allocation leaving one die corner weakly fed
Power-gating switch fabric undersized

items.classic_trap: treating the failure as generic slow silicon and hammering global optimization or a blanket derate, instead of locating the droop and fixing the grid locally — the timing fix then never converges because the true mechanism is voltage, not delay
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, lower Vdd and higher interconnect resistance make IR sensitivity far worse, so voltage-aware per-instance timing is mandatory; at 28nm static IR signoff usually caught it

items.symptom: Clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: Histogram insertion delay per sink, grouped by clock and by hierarchy level
first_checks.why_first: cheapest report and it immediately splits 'a few outlier sinks' from 'an entire subtree shifted late'

first_checks.check: Check whether outlier sinks sit in don't-touch regions, inside macros, or near excluded/pre-routed clock resources
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most common structural cause — CTS never allowed to fix those sinks — in one query

first_checks.check: Diff the sink list in the CTS spec against the current netlist
first_checks.why_first: a stale or mis-excluded sink list produces exactly this symptom and takes minutes to confirm

first_checks.check: Overlay outlier locations on the congestion map
first_checks.why_first: if late sinks coincide with routed detours, clock-net congestion is implicated before any rerun

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Manually route or buffer one outlier sink's clock net with unrestricted resources
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: insertion delay dropping to target confirms routing congestion/blockage on that net as the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: delay staying high even with a clean dedicated route excludes routing and confirms structural depth or placement distance

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Find the common ancestor of all late sinks and measure pre-existing delay through it
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: one CG cell or mux whose output feeds only the late group with a long input net confirms branch-level imbalance at a single structure
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no shared structure among outliers excludes a single-tree defect and points at per-sink placement

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare physical distance from clock root to outliers vs to the median sink
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: outliers sitting at the far edge of a macro cluster or die corner confirms inherent placement-driven latency
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: outliers interleaved physically with on-target sinks excludes placement distance as the driver

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run CTS with congestion-aware clock routing enabled (or the region decongested) and compare the tail
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: tail collapsing confirms congestion-driven divergence
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: tail persisting excludes congestion and leaves buffering/topology causes

common_root_causes.cause: Sink clusters placed late at die/macro edges, far from the tree root
Clock nets blocked by obstructions, NDRs, or pre-routes forcing detours
Stale or wrong CTS sink/exclude list
Deep gating/mux chains on one branch adding levels of delay
Sink count ballooned after a late netlist change without re-running CTS

items.classic_trap: padding delay onto all the on-time sinks to match the late outliers — inflating total latency, power, and area — when relocating the outlier cluster or clearing one blocked route fixes the tail at its root
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, CTS runs corner-aware with OCV-derated clock paths and larger latency budgets, so the 'skew target' itself is multi-corner; at 28nm a single balanced tree was typically sufficient

items.symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: Read the mismatch summary counts first — net count, device count, and the open/short/missing breakdown — before opening any single mismatch
first_checks.why_first: cheapest step, and the classic arithmetic (one real short typically surfaces as a short plus a paired open) can collapse dozens of reported mismatches into one physical defect

first_checks.check: Run a dedicated power/ground short check
first_checks.why_first: most shorts are signal-to-rail at a via, and rail involvement is both most common and cheapest to confirm

first_checks.check: Cross-probe one representative mismatch between layout and schematic viewers
first_checks.why_first: one manually verified case establishes whether the reports are real geometry problems or label/mapping artifacts

first_checks.check: Diff the netlist and GDS versions against the last clean LVS run
first_checks.why_first: if mismatches track a recent ECO or block integration, the search space shrinks to that delta immediately

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run LVS per sub-block and compare against full-chip results
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: sub-blocks clean but full chip failing confirms top-level integration wiring or PG stitching as the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: the owning sub-block itself failing excludes top-level wiring and localizes the defect inside the block

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Audit text/label completeness on the flagged nets (labels vs geometry check)
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: geometry continuous but labels missing confirms a label-driven phantom open
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: labels present and correct on all flagged nets excludes label artifacts — the open or short is physical

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Cut the suspect via/wire locally in a trial GDS edit and re-run LVS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: mismatch counts changing in the predicted direction confirms that via/wire was the defect
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: mismatch counts unchanged excludes the suspect and the defect is elsewhere in the flagged set

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-extract with via-recognition/layer-mapping options reset to the foundry default
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: opens vanishing under default recognition confirms a techfile or recognition misconfiguration, not a layout defect
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: opens persisting under defaults excludes recognition artifacts

common_root_causes.cause: PG rail/strap shorts or missing PG vias
Dropped via cuts or incomplete via arrays on signal nets
Block-boundary integration wiring errors (cross-block nets)
Missing labels/text producing phantom opens

items.classic_trap: grinding through every reported mismatch individually; veterans first apply the short/open pairing heuristic — fix one real short and its paired 'open' report typically disappears with it, collapsing the work by an order of magnitude
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, LVS additionally checks mask-ops/coloring and richer via structures, so some 'shorts' are coloring violations that 28nm never saw

items.symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: Diff the device summary tables — counts and W/L (or fin-count) histograms by device type — between extraction and source netlist
first_checks.why_first: cheapest step and it instantly separates 'every device of a type is scaled' (systematic/version issue) from 'a handful of outliers' (local edits)

first_checks.check: Classify the 'extra' devices by master cell name
first_checks.why_first: if extras are all fill/decap/dummy or ESD/antenna devices, the cause is known in one sort

first_checks.check: Cross-reference mismatched devices against the recent ECO/change log
first_checks.why_first: mismatch tracking a known edit rules out library-level causes immediately

first_checks.check: Check the LVS device-merge (parallel/series combining) settings in both runs
first_checks.why_first: mismatched merge configuration fabricates size mismatches from identical layout — cheapest config check before suspecting geometry

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run LVS with parallel-device merging toggled (on vs off) between the two views
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: mismatches collapsing under the changed merge setting confirms a configuration artifact, not a layout error
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: mismatches invariant to merge setting excludes this class and confirms real size/device differences

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Regenerate the source netlist from the same library/PDK version as the layout and re-run
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: mismatches vanishing confirms library-version skew as the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: mismatches persisting against the matched-version netlist excludes version skew and indicts the layout edits themselves

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Update the netlist to include (or exclude) the physically inserted fill/dummy/ESD devices and re-run
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: extras reconciling after netlist update confirms 'physical additions never back-annotated' as the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: unexplained devices remaining after reconciliation are true layout defects to chase individually

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Vary device-recognition bounds in extraction
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: phantom devices appearing or disappearing with recognition bounds confirms device-recognition (not geometry) as the mechanism
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: device set stable across recognition settings excludes recognition artifacts

common_root_causes.cause: Source netlist stale relative to the layout (ECO applied to one side only)
Fill/decap/dummy/ESD devices inserted in layout without netlist update
Library version skew between layout cells and source netlist
Device-merge or recognition option differences between runs

items.classic_trap: assuming layout is wrong and redrawing devices for days, when the source netlist was stale or the merge options differed — veterans check the two 'free' explanations before touching geometry
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, devices are discrete fin-count/fixed-rule structures checked against discrete size steps, so 'wrong size' means wrong cell variant or fin count rather than a continuous W/L typo as at 28nm

items.symptom: Antenna (process-antenna-effect) violations at signoff

first_checks.check: Group the antenna report by metal layer and by rule type (per-layer ratio vs cumulative ratio)
first_checks.why_first: cheapest split — violations concentrated on one long-trunk layer point at jumpers, while cumulative failures point at total metal run

first_checks.check: For each violating net, check whether a jumper (route-up) or antenna diode already exists nearby
first_checks.why_first: rules out 'fix exists but was lost or misplaced' before any new fix is designed

first_checks.check: Check the antenna rule deck version and gate-area accounting mode against the foundry signoff requirement
first_checks.why_first: a stale deck or a pessimistic default gate-area assumption can manufacture the entire violation set

first_checks.check: Correlate violating nets with high-fanout and long-span nets (clock, reset, scan)
first_checks.why_first: confirms the physical intuition — long unbroken trunks to big gate loads — in one overlay

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Apply jumpers (route up a layer near the gate) to a sample of violating nets and re-run the antenna check
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: sampled nets clearing without diodes confirms jumper-fix sufficiency and that trunk length was the mechanism
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: ratio still failing after jumping excludes trunk-length-only explanation and demands diodes or gate protection

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run with the current foundry antenna ratio tables and extraction-based gate area enabled
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violation count collapsing confirms the earlier set was a stale-deck or pessimistic-gate-area artifact
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations persisting under current rules and real gate area excludes rule-deck artifacts — fixes are genuinely required

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run both per-layer and cumulative ratio modes separately
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: failing only in cumulative mode confirms total accumulated metal as the driver, so fixes must shorten total run, not one layer
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: failing only per-layer confines the problem to specific layer segments and excludes cumulative effects

common_root_causes.cause: Long un-jumpered trunks on upper metals
Antenna repair disabled or lost during a routing/ECO stage and never rechecked
Missing antenna diodes near high-fanout gate loads
Stale ratio tables or pessimistic gate-area defaults

items.classic_trap: sprinkling antenna diodes on every violating net — diodes cost area and add leakage, while jumpers are nearly free; or fixing antenna mid-flow and then losing the fixes in a later ECO without re-running the check at signoff
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below the rule decks are stricter with cumulative ratios and extraction-based gate-area accounting across more layers; at 28nm a handful of diodes typically sufficed

items.symptom: Detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Cluster the detail-route violations by rule type (via spacing vs wire spacing vs width) and by layer
first_checks.why_first: cheapest split — via-rule clusters point at pin access, wire-rule clusters at mid-route congestion or obstructions

first_checks.check: Check whether violations sit at cell pins (access conflicts) or mid-wire
first_checks.why_first: at advanced nodes pin access is the dominant cause and this single observation redirects the entire investigation

first_checks.check: List NDR nets and pre-routes/PG straps crossing the hotspot
first_checks.why_first: rules out self-induced rule conflicts and fixed obstructions before blaming the router

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-route the hotspot region with pin-access effort/optimization maximized
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violations clearing confirms pin-access as the mechanism (cell rows or library pins need adjustment)
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations persisting at maximal pin-access effort excludes access and confirms a genuine space conflict

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Allow the router freedom to detour involved nets to upper layers within the hotspot
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violations relocating away from the spot confirms a local vertical/track resource conflict the router can route around
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations pinned to the same coordinates regardless of detour freedom confirm a fixed obstruction (strap, pre-route, via stack) that must be physically changed

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Strip NDRs from the involved nets in a trial route of the region
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRCs vanishing confirms NDR-induced conflicts with neighbors
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: DRCs persisting without NDRs excludes rule-driven conflicts

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run the same region with a different route order/seed
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: hotspot relocating with seed confirms order-dependent congestion rather than hard geometry
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: hotspot invariant to seed confirms a geometry-bound conflict independent of routing order

common_root_causes.cause: Pin-access conflicts in dense cell rows
Pre-routes/PG straps pinching tracks through the region
NDR nets adjacent to default-rule nets
Local congestion finer-grained than the global-route grid caught

items.classic_trap: assuming 'clean global route' means congestion is ruled out and blaming the detailed router — when the actual hotspot is pin access, which no amount of re-running the router fixes without touching cell placement or the library pins
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, pin access with color-aware pins and restricted via choices dominates detail-route DRCs; at 28nm hotspots were mostly plain congestion

items.symptom: Unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Do the density arithmetic: total cell area + macro area + halos + blockages against die area at the current target utilization
first_checks.why_first: cheapest check of all — most 'divergence' is simply a design that does not fit at the requested density

first_checks.check: Map macro/hard-block locations, halos, and the contiguous routable channels remaining between them
first_checks.why_first: one badly placed macro row can sever the die and cause region overflow no global tuning recovers

first_checks.check: Find extreme-fanout nets (scan chains, resets, ties) and their placement contribution
first_checks.why_first: mega-nets dominate wirelength and can prevent convergence; identifying them is a single sorted report

first_checks.check: Inventory fixed cells, don't-touch regions, and placement blockages as a fraction of usable area
first_checks.why_first: rules out 'the die is nominally big enough but effectively full' in one query

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Raise the density target ceiling (or set a per-region target) and rerun placement
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: convergence at higher density confirms the target — not the netlist or macros — was the blocker
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: divergence persisting even at high density excludes pure utilization and confirms structural causes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run with macros pre-placed by hand or per a channel plan, versus free macro placement
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: convergence with pre-placed macros confirms automatic macro arrangement as the diverging factor
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: divergence persisting with manual macro placement excludes macro placement and shifts suspicion to netlist/obstacles

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Virtual-weight or detach the mega-nets (e.g., break scan order) and rerun
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: convergence returning confirms mega-net wirelength domination as the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no improvement excludes net weighting and leaves density/obstacle causes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Examine the overflow map at divergence: concentrated region vs uniform overflow
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: overflow concentrated around one obstacle or macro halo confirms a local structural conflict
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: uniform overflow across the die confirms global utilization, not local geometry

common_root_causes.cause: Utilization target physically unachievable (die too small or blockages too large)
Macro arrangement leaving insufficient channels/halos
Huge-fanout nets (scan, reset) dominating placement cost
Excessive fixed obstacles/don't-touch regions fragmenting usable area
Netlist defects (unconnected pins, overlapping instances)

items.classic_trap: treating divergence as a tool bug and cycling placer options/effort knobs, when the density arithmetic on a napkin already showed the design cannot fit as constrained — teams lose days on knobs that no setting can overcome
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, achievable utilization is lower because PG and routing resources eat more tracks, so a density that 'worked at 28nm' silently fails at 7nm even with the same die area

items.symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Inspect global-route congestion map hotspots vs. local density reports
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest visual check that rules out pure density overflow versus pin/access or cell-shape issues

first_checks.check: Count and map hard macros, blockages, and keep-out zones near the DRC clusters
first_checks.why_first: Rules out placement legality artifacts that density metrics ignore

first_checks.check: Examine pin density and cell orientation distributions in the failing regions
first_checks.why_first: Discriminates access-limited congestion from pure track shortage

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily inflate cell spacing or add soft blockages only in the hotspot cells and re-run global route
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRCs vanish → local pin/access or orientation packing was the driver
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: DRCs persist → deeper track or layer-resource shortage

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare congestion after forcing all standard cells to preferred orientation vs. mixed
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Congestion drops sharply with preferred orientation → orientation-induced access conflict
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: No change → orientation not causal

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Disable or upsize metal-layer preferred-direction constraints on the congested layers and re-route
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRCs clear → preferred-direction or via-ladder restriction was binding
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Still congested → true capacity shortfall

common_root_causes.cause: High pin-density standard-cell clusters or multi-height cells creating local access conflicts
Hard-macro abutment or channel pinch-offs invisible to average density metrics
Overly aggressive power-grid or via-ladder reservation eating routing tracks
Placement legalization that packed cells into narrow corridors after density check

items.classic_trap: Treating average or bin density as sufficient and missing local pin-access or orientation hotspots
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below pin-access and multi-patterning constraints make orientation and cut-mask rules far more frequent drivers than at 28nm

items.symptom: setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Diff pre-CTS vs post-CTS timing on the same paths and isolate the delta to clock path or data path
first_checks.why_first: Immediately separates pure data-path regression from clock-insertion or skew change

first_checks.check: Extract the common clock-path segments shared by all failing endpoints
first_checks.why_first: Rules out global clock-tree problem versus scattered data-path issues

first_checks.check: Check useful-skew and latency targets versus achieved insertion delays on the failing clocks
first_checks.why_first: Cheap confirmation that CTS met (or missed) the intended balancing

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If all failing paths share one clock-gating or buffer cell, replace or upsize only that cell and re-time; else spread the same experiment across unrelated hierarchies
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Shared cell fix clears all → that cell is the bottleneck; spread fix needed → distributed data-path or multiple clock domains
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Opposite pattern excludes the single-cell hypothesis

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Force ideal clocks (zero skew, zero latency) on the failing domains and re-report setup
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Violations disappear → clock-tree insertion/skew is causal
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Violations remain → pure data-path delay increase

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare setup slack when useful-skew is disabled versus enabled on the same CTS result
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Slack recovers only with useful skew → intentional skew was required but not realized
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: No difference → useful-skew not the missing ingredient

common_root_causes.cause: CTS inserted extra latency or unbalanced skew that eroded setup margin
Clock-gating or enable logic on the critical path became slower after buffering
Data-path cells detoured or were resized sub-optimally during post-CTS optimization
OCV/AOCV derates applied more pessimistically after real clock tree existed

items.classic_trap: Blaming data-path cells when the entire slack loss is in the newly inserted clock path
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below AOCV/POCV and multi-corner CTS make clock-path contribution larger and more variable than typical 28nm flows

items.symptom: hold (min-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Identify whether failing paths are short data paths between closely placed flops on the same clock
first_checks.why_first: Most common and cheapest pattern to confirm

first_checks.check: Measure actual clock skew (including local) on the launch/capture pairs of the violators
first_checks.why_first: Rules out excessive positive skew introduced by CTS

first_checks.check: Check hold derates, clock uncertainty, and any intentional useful skew that became harmful
first_checks.why_first: Quickly isolates constraint versus physical causes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If violators share a common local clock buffer, upsize or rebuffer only that branch; if they are scattered, apply uniform hold buffers on data paths
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Shared-buffer fix clears the cluster → local skew source; scattered data-path buffers needed → pure min-delay shortfall
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Opposite result excludes the clustered-skew hypothesis

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run hold analysis with zero clock uncertainty and minimum derates
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Violations vanish → constraint pessimism was dominant
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Violations remain → real physical min-delay problem

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Force the same insertion delay on launch and capture clocks for the failing pairs and re-report
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Holds clear → skew introduced by CTS is causal
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Holds persist → data-path delay too small independent of skew

common_root_causes.cause: Short data paths between adjacent flops combined with residual positive skew
CTS useful-skew or balancing that favored setup at the expense of hold
Insufficient hold buffers inserted because pre-CTS hold was optimistic
Local clock skew from uneven clock-gate or buffer loading

items.classic_trap: Over-buffering the data path globally when only a few local clock branches need balancing
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below hold windows shrink and variation increases, making post-CTS hold more frequent and more sensitive to local skew than at 28nm

items.symptom: IR-drop-induced timing failure

first_checks.check: Map the failing timing endpoints onto the dynamic or static IR-drop hotspots
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest spatial correlation that confirms or refutes voltage-drop causality

first_checks.check: Compare timing slack with ideal voltage versus the IR-drop-aware voltage map
first_checks.why_first: Quantifies how much of the violation is voltage-induced

first_checks.check: Inspect power-grid density, via counts, and package bump proximity in the hotspot
first_checks.why_first: Rules out obvious grid or packaging weaknesses

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Scale the local supply voltage of only the IR-hotspot instances by the measured drop and re-time; leave other instances ideal
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Violations appear or worsen only on the scaled instances → IR is causal for those paths
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: No change → timing failure independent of the observed drop

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Add temporary decap or widen power straps only under the failing cluster and re-analyze both IR and timing
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Both IR and timing improve → local grid weakness was the link
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: IR improves but timing does not → timing root is elsewhere

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Vector the highest-activity switching windows that coincide with the timing paths and re-run dynamic IR
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Peak drop aligns with the failing paths → activity-induced dynamic IR
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Peak drop elsewhere → static or unrelated dynamic issue

common_root_causes.cause: Insufficient local power-grid density or via stacking under high-activity logic
Simultaneous switching of wide buses or clock gates creating transient droop
Package or bump placement far from the demand hotspot
Overly aggressive power-gating or weak header devices

items.classic_trap: Assuming any IR hotspot automatically explains the timing path without checking spatial and temporal overlap
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below lower Vdd and higher current density make dynamic IR far more frequent and tighter to timing than typical 28nm designs

items.symptom: clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: Plot achieved versus target insertion delay for every sink and identify outlier clusters
first_checks.why_first: Immediate visual separation of global versus local divergence

first_checks.check: Check clock-tree topology reports for missing or blocked buffer sites near the outliers
first_checks.why_first: Rules out placement or blockage obstacles to buffering

first_checks.check: Verify clock-root latency, generated-clock definitions, and any multi-corner target conflicts
first_checks.why_first: Excludes constraint or multi-mode mis-specification

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If outliers share a common upstream buffer or region, force extra buffer levels only on that branch; if outliers are scattered, relax global latency targets
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Branch fix equalizes the cluster → local blockage or loading; global relax needed → overall target infeasible
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Opposite pattern excludes the local-branch hypothesis

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Remove all placement blockages and keep-outs in the outlier regions and re-run CTS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Targets met → physical blockage prevented proper buffering
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Still diverge → capacity, library, or constraint issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run CTS with a single corner/mode versus the full multi-corner set and compare sink latency spread
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Single-corner meets targets, multi-corner diverges → conflicting multi-corner constraints
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Both diverge equally → not a multi-corner conflict

common_root_causes.cause: Placement blockages or macro keep-outs preventing buffer insertion on some branches
Highly unbalanced sink loads or clock-gate clustering
Overly tight or conflicting multi-corner insertion-delay targets
Insufficient buffer library variety or drive-strength steps

items.classic_trap: Loosening global skew targets when only a few local branches are blocked
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below CTS must also satisfy multi-patterning and via-pillar constraints, increasing divergence frequency versus 28nm

items.symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: Cross-reference the LVS error locations against the corresponding layout and schematic net names
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest way to see whether the mismatch is naming, extraction, or real connectivity

first_checks.check: Inspect the extracted netlist for floating pins, unlabeled metal, or unintended merges near the reported short/open
first_checks.why_first: Rules out pure extraction artifacts

first_checks.check: Check hierarchical versus flat LVS results on the same cell
first_checks.why_first: Discriminates hierarchy boundary problems from true geometry issues

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If the shorted nets belong to different power domains or intended isolated signals, examine the geometry at their closest approach; if they are the same logical net, check for missing via or label
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Different nets touching → real short; same net missing connection → real open
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Geometry clean → extraction or labeling error

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-extract with connectivity-only versus full parasitic extraction and re-run LVS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Connectivity-only clean, full extraction fails → parasitic or marker issue; both fail → geometric connectivity problem
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Opposite result narrows the cause

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Promote the failing hierarchical block to flat and re-LVS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Flat LVS passes → hierarchy or pin-mismatch problem
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Flat still fails → real layout versus schematic discrepancy

common_root_causes.cause: Missing or misaligned vias between metal layers
Unintended metal shorts from over-enclosures or fill
Hierarchical pin or net-name mismatches at block boundaries
Extraction tool missing a device or net because of labeling or soft-check settings

items.classic_trap: Assuming every LVS short is a real geometry error when many are hierarchical naming or extraction-setting artifacts
items.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

items.symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: Compare the reported device parameters (width, length, fingers, multiplier) between layout extraction and schematic
first_checks.why_first: Directly quantifies the size discrepancy

first_checks.check: Inspect the layout for unintended device recognition (e.g., extra poly or diffusion islands)
first_checks.why_first: Rules out extraction creating phantom devices

first_checks.check: Verify schematic source versus the netlist actually used for LVS (including any generated or parameterized cells)
first_checks.why_first: Excludes schematic-side version skew

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If extra devices appear only in extraction, mask or remove the suspicious geometry and re-extract; if sizes differ, force the layout device to schematic dimensions and re-LVS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Extra-device errors clear after geometry edit → phantom recognition; size errors clear after forced match → real drawn-size mismatch
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Errors persist → deeper rule or tool issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run LVS with device-recognition rules relaxed versus strict and compare extra-device counts
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Extras disappear with relaxed rules → over-aggressive recognition
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Extras remain → true extra geometry

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare LVS using the original schematic versus a schematic regenerated from the layout
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Regenerated matches layout → original schematic was stale or parameterized incorrectly
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Both mismatch → layout itself is wrong

common_root_causes.cause: Layout drawn with incorrect width/length or finger count relative to schematic
Extraction recognizing dummy or fill structures as active devices
Parameterized or PCell expansion mismatch between schematic and layout views
Stale schematic netlist used for LVS after layout ECO

items.classic_trap: Editing the schematic to match a wrong layout instead of correcting the drawn device geometry
items.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

items.symptom: antenna (process-antenna-effect) violations at signoff

first_checks.check: Map the violating nets and identify the largest metal area ratio relative to the gate or diffusion area
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest confirmation of classic area-ratio antenna

first_checks.check: Check whether diode insertion or metal-jump (layer hopping) rules were enabled in the router
first_checks.why_first: Rules out simple missing-fix-option causes

first_checks.check: Inspect long top-metal routes that land on small gates without intermediate discharge paths
first_checks.why_first: Common physical pattern

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Insert antenna diodes only on the violating pins and re-check; if still failing, force a metal-layer jump on the same nets
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Diode clears → classic charge accumulation; jump needed → diode insufficient or rule forbids diode
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Neither helps → extraction or rule-deck mismatch

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Break the longest violating metal segment into two by adding a via to a lower layer and back, then re-run antenna check
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Violation clears → pure area-ratio problem solvable by hopping
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Still violates → partial antenna or cumulative multi-layer issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare antenna results with foundry rule deck versus a relaxed internal deck
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Only foundry deck fails → rule interpretation or margin difference
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Both fail equally → real geometric violation

common_root_causes.cause: Long upper-metal routes connected to small gate poly without intermediate vias or diodes
Router antenna-prevention options (diode insertion, hopping) left disabled or constrained too tightly
Cumulative antenna from multiple layers that individually look safe
ECO routes that bypassed the original antenna-aware path

items.classic_trap: Inserting diodes everywhere when a simple metal hop would have been cheaper and sufficient
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below multi-patterning and thinner gate oxides make antenna rules stricter and diode insertion more constrained than at 28nm

items.symptom: detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Overlay the detailed DRC locations on the global-route congestion and track-usage maps
first_checks.why_first: Confirms whether global route was truly clean or merely averaged away local problems

first_checks.check: Inspect via spacing, end-of-line, and cut-mask rules in the hotspot layers
first_checks.why_first: Many post-global DRCs are via or coloring rule violations invisible to global route

first_checks.check: Check for pin-access or cell-boundary conflicts that global route treated as soft
first_checks.why_first: Common source of localized detailed failures

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If DRCs cluster around vias or pin access, force alternative via structures or pin swaps only in that region; if they follow long routes, relax spacing or widen tracks locally
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Via/pin fix clears → access or via-rule problem; track relax needed → capacity or spacing rule binding
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Opposite result excludes the hypothesized class

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run detailed route with via-pillar or multi-cut vias disabled versus enabled
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRCs appear only with advanced vias → via-rule or enclosure conflict
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: DRCs identical → not via-structure related

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Increase local track allocation or reduce adjacent cell density and re-detail-route only the hotspot
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRCs clear → residual local capacity shortfall that global route missed
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Still fail → pure design-rule (non-capacity) violation

common_root_causes.cause: Via spacing, enclosure, or cut-mask coloring violations invisible to global routing
Pin-access conflicts on multi-height or complex standard cells
Local track shortage after power-grid or blockage finalization
End-of-line or minimum-area metal rules triggered by short jogs

items.classic_trap: Re-running global route with higher effort when the real problem is detailed via or coloring rules
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below multi-patterning, EUV, and via-pillar rules create far more detailed-only DRCs than classic 28nm double-patterning

items.symptom: unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Examine the overflow or divergence metric progression across global-placement iterations
first_checks.why_first: Shows whether the engine is oscillating, stuck, or steadily worsening

first_checks.check: Map the densest bins against macros, blockages, and fixed-cell regions
first_checks.why_first: Rules out obvious floorplan-induced unroutability

first_checks.check: Compare target density, max utilization, and any density screens versus achieved
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest constraint-versus-result check

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If overflow is concentrated near macros, inflate macro keep-outs or move macros; if overflow is uniform, lower global density target or inflate all cells
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Macro move clears → floorplan pinch; global density reduction needed → pure capacity shortfall
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Opposite pattern excludes the hypothesized class

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run placement with all soft blockages and density screens removed versus fully constrained
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Unconstrained succeeds, constrained fails → blockage or screen over-constraint
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Both fail → fundamental area or cell-count problem

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Replace high-pin-count or large-area cells with smaller equivalents (or remove a non-critical hierarchy) and re-place
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Placement converges → those cells were the packing bottleneck
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Still diverges → broader floorplan or utilization issue

common_root_causes.cause: Floorplan channels or macro placements that create unroutable narrow corridors
Target utilization set higher than the design’s real packing limit given cell mix
Excessive fixed cells, soft blockages, or density screens over-constraining the placer
Pathological cell size mix (many large multi-height cells) preventing legal packing

items.classic_trap: Raising placement effort or runtime when the floorplan itself is the fundamental bottleneck
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below multi-height cells and stricter pin-access rules make packing failures more frequent than typical 28nm standard-cell libraries

items.symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Inspect macro pin access patterns and orientations for track blockage
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most common cause with visual inspection

first_checks.check: Review routing layer utilization map for resource starvation
first_checks.why_first: cheapest report to confirm if raw tracks are exhausted

first_checks.check: Check for multi-patterning coloring conflicts in DRC hotspot
first_checks.why_first: distinguishes advanced-node-specific issue from generic congestion

first_checks.check: Verify cell spacing constraints in dense standard-cell rows
first_checks.why_first: eliminates simple density-rule violation before deep debugging

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily remove macro pin-access blockages from routing constraints and re-route
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRCs shift to macro edges or reduce significantly → macro pin access is the root cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: DRCs remain in std-cell regions unchanged → not macro pin access, investigate std-cell density or track starvation

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Increase global routing track utilization target by order of 10% and re-route
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRC count decreases significantly → routing resource shortage
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: DRC count unchanged → pin access or coloring issue, not raw resource shortage

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Force single-cut vias throughout the design and re-run detailed route
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRCs reduce → via-array spacing or multi-cut enclosure issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: DRCs unchanged → not via-related, investigate metal track or pin access

common_root_causes.cause: Macro pin access conflicts blocking adjacent tracks
Macro placement orientation creating channel blockage
Routing layer utilization imbalance starving specific layers
Cell spacing violations in dense standard-cell rows

items.classic_trap: Blaming placement density when the issue is actually macro pin access or orientation
items.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, FinFET complex pin shapes and multi-patterning coloring constraints dominate, whereas at 28nm macro blockage and track availability were primary

items.symptom: setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Report clock skew on all failing timing paths
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most common post-CTS setup failure mode

first_checks.check: Identify common clock gating cells shared across failing paths
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to find localized insertion-delay imbalance

first_checks.check: Verify OCV and derate settings applied to analysis
first_checks.why_first: eliminates systematic margin pessimism before physical debugging

first_checks.check: Run timing with ideal clocks zeroing insertion delay and skew
first_checks.why_first: definitively separates clock problem from data path in minutes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run static timing analysis with ideal clocks removing all insertion delay and skew
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: All violations disappear → clock skew or insertion delay is the root cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Violations remain with similar magnitude → data path problem, not clock

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if every failing path passes through a specific clock gating cell
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Yes → clock gating insertion delay imbalance is the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: No, spread across unrelated hierarchies → broader skew or data path issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Measure actual skew on each failing path relative to clock period
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Skew exceeds order of 15-20% of clock period → skew-dominated failure
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Skew is small relative to period → data path delay dominates

items.node_era_note: At 28nm hold fixed with small delay cells; at 7nm-and-below min-delay variation and low-track high resistance requires careful LVT vs hold buffer tradeoff and CCT

items.symptom: IR-drop-induced timing failure

first_checks.check: Overlay dynamic IR-drop heatmap with failing timing path physical locations
first_checks.why_first: cheapest correlation that rules in power vs pure timing

first_checks.check: Check static IR and PG connectivity: missing vias on straps, narrow straps, via pillar drops
first_checks.why_first: rules out most common grid weakness before vector analysis

first_checks.check: Check switching activity assumptions: vectorless toggle rate vs VCD/FSDB-based activity in hotspot
first_checks.why_first: prevents over or under estimation of dynamic droop

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun timing with ideal 100% VDD / decoupled power (set power net to ideal): if slack improves by order of 30-100ps at low Vdd nodes vs <5ps change
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: IR-induced if large improvement with ideal power
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: pure timing / cell sizing if negligible change

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If failures cluster in same time window and same power domain as high toggle bus (e.g., 64-bit datapath switching) vs static IR map alone aligns without temporal correlation
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: dynamic IR / simultaneous switching if temporal clustering
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: static grid weakness if aligns with static map regardless of switching window

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare slack with and without decap cells / with increased bump pitch near hotspot: if adding decap or moving activity away recovers
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: decap shortage / bump distance if recovers
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: insufficient strap width if decap does not help but widening straps does

common_root_causes.cause: Insufficient PG mesh / strap width / via count causing high resistance to C4 bump
High simultaneous switching activity cluster: wide bus, clock gating, multiplier bank
Package bump / C4 placement far from high-current hotspot, long lateral path
Insufficient decap / filler decap removed, low intrinsic decap of cells
Power gating / EM limits causing intentional strap thinning not modeled in timing

items.classic_trap: Fixing timing by upsizing cells in IR hotspot, which increases current and makes IR drop worse, leading to power spiral
items.node_era_note: At 28nm static IR with ~20-30mV droop dominated; at 7nm-and-below dynamic IR with order of 60-120mV transient droop due to thin BEOL and high current density dominates

items.symptom: clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: Plot skew histogram, insertion delay vs target, and max transition / cap per clock level
first_checks.why_first: cheapest quantitative view of divergence

first_checks.check: Report clock routing blockages and congestion map on clock layers
first_checks.why_first: rules out resource blocking before tweaking targets

first_checks.check: Check sink capacitance imbalance: gated vs ungated, macro pins vs flop pins, NDRs
first_checks.why_first: most common topology reason for non-convergence

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If skew outliers all share same physical region or same blockage box / macro channel, vs outliers scattered randomly with no spatial correlation
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: routing blockage / congestion cause if spatially clustered
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: capacitance imbalance / gating imbalance if scattered random

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun CTS with non-default-rule clock routing widened / double-spaced or with extra layer allowed: if divergence drops >30%
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: clock NDR / routing constraint too tight
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: unrealistic insertion delay targets if still diverges with relaxed rules

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare latency target vs actual longest / shortest root-to-sink: if one tail cannot meet target even with zero skew, vs both tails can meet but skew cannot close
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: unrealistic target / floorplan stretch if one tail impossible
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: skew balancing algorithm issue if both tails feasible but skew large

common_root_causes.cause: Highly unbalanced clock topology: large clock-gating tree vs ungated, macro clock pins with huge cap
Routing blockages, macro halos, or congestion forcing detours on clock trunks
Unrealistic insertion delay / skew targets, especially cross-domain or with long IO clocks
Max transition / max cap violations on clock nets causing CTS to upsize detour
Clock tree topology constraint: dont_touch, fixed buffers, or wrong inverters in clock path

items.classic_trap: Tightening skew target further when insertion delay target is unachievable, causing CTS to iterate without convergence
items.node_era_note: At 28nm single corner CTS often converged; at 7nm-and-below multi-corner, OCV, and via variation require useful-skew and concurrent multi-mode CTS

items.symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: Read LVS report: net count diff, short list, open list, and property error summary
first_checks.why_first: cheapest classification of error type

first_checks.check: Run short locator and open locator, overlay marker with layout text labels
first_checks.why_first: pinpoints geometry vs labeling

first_checks.check: Check extraction options: virtual connect, label depth, text purpose mapping
first_checks.why_first: rules out deck setup before editing geometry

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If one layout net is merged from multiple schematic nets with overlap at label or text near cell boundary, vs metal overlap far from any label with same layer polygon merging
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: label / text short or text purpose wrong if near label
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: true metal short if far from labels with physical polygon overlap

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If open shows same net name on both sides of port but port layer off-grid or 0.5*track off, vs open inside cell with missing via enclosure
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: port alignment / off-grid or hierarchy port mapping issue if at boundary
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: missing via / wrong layer map if inside cell

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Toggle virtual connect and texted vs geometry connect: if short disappears with no virtual connect
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: virtual connection / label depth causing false short
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: physical short if persists without virtual connect

common_root_causes.cause: Label / text placement: duplicate names, wrong purpose, text shorting two nets
Off-grid pins, misaligned hierarchy ports, or 45-degree / off-manufacturing-grid geometry
Missing via / layer mapping in extraction deck, or wrong layer purpose for recognition
Floating fill / metal fill shorting or connecting through fill due to missing fill exclusion
Schematic vs layout hierarchy mismatch: extra level of hierarchy or bus bit naming mismatch

items.classic_trap: Editing schematic to match false layout short from label instead of fixing label purpose or text layer, embedding error
items.node_era_note: At 28nm single patterning shorts simple; at 7nm-and-below color-aware LVS and multi-patterning requires color-correct labels and color-aware short locator

items.symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: Report device parameter diff: W, L, fin count, multiplier m, and count by device type
first_checks.why_first: cheapest to classify size vs count

first_checks.check: Check schematic vs layout parallel/series merging options and property tolerance
first_checks.why_first: rules out merging mismatch before PDK hunt

first_checks.check: Check recognition layer mapping: diffusion, poly, nwell, pwell purpose pairs for device
first_checks.why_first: most common PDK setup error

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If extra devices are all same type in filler / decap / tie-cell area, vs extra devices scattered with random sizes in core
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: filler / decap / tie cells not blackboxed or excluded if clustered in filler
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: recognition layer mapping issue if random scattered

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If W mismatch is integer multiple (2x, 4x) of expected vs small continuous delta (e.g., 5-10% due to LOD)
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: parallel device merging / folding or m-factor mismatch if integer multiple
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: LOD / stress or extraction tolerance if small continuous delta

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Toggle device recognition: check if device disappears when nudging poly extension or diffusion overlap by small dbu: indicates marginal recognition
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: marginal device recognition / DRC-clean but LVS-failing edge length
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: schematic property error if device still recognized with correct size

common_root_causes.cause: Incorrect recognition layer or purpose mapping, or missing marker layer for LVS device
Schematic multiplier m, parallel fingers, or folding mismatch vs layout (e.g., 2x vs 1x with m=2)
Filler, decap, antenna diode, or tie cells included in extraction not excluded as devices
Property tolerance too tight for LOD, WPE, or fin variation vs schematic without PEX
Schematic with dummy devices or ESD devices that have no layout counterpart

items.classic_trap: Assuming extraction bug when root is schematic m-factor or parallel merge option causing intentional size difference
items.node_era_note: At 28nm width/length mapping simple; at 7nm-and-below FinFET requires fin count vs width mapping and fin-grid alignment causing size mismatch

items.symptom: antenna (process-antenna-effect) violations at signoff

first_checks.check: Report antenna ratio by layer, cumulative vs layer-specific, and gate area per violation
first_checks.why_first: cheapest classification of layer and accumulation type

first_checks.check: Check diode / antenna cell availability and max distance rule in library
first_checks.why_first: rules out missing protection before rerouting

first_checks.check: Plot violation location vs long net bounding box: identify long parallel runs on M1-M3
first_checks.why_first: identifies long floating net root quickly

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If violations cluster on long M1/M2 nets feeding single minimum-size inverter with no diode within antenna max distance, vs violations on higher metals (M4+) with large cumulative area
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: local discharge path / diode distance issue if low-metal single gate
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: accumulated antenna area ratio if high-metal large area

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Try jumper insertion (break long net to upper metal) vs diode insertion only: if >90% fix with jumper layer hop vs <20% fix
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: long parallel run without hopping if jumper fixes
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: needs diode protection if jumper does not fix but diode does

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if violation disappears when routing with antenna-aware router or with enforced layer hopping every N um
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: router not antenna-aware or not doing layer hopping
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: PDK antenna ratio too conservative or gate area miscalculation if still violates with hopping

common_root_causes.cause: Long floating metal on low layers connected to small gate without discharge path
Missing antenna diode / antenna cell or max diode distance violated
Router not inserting enough layer jumps / insufficient metal hopping for long nets
Large macro pin or top-level pin with huge metal area feeding small gate
Antenna rule deck using cumulative ratio that accumulates across hierarchy incorrectly

items.classic_trap: Fixing all violations by inserting diodes everywhere, adding leakage and cap, instead of using jumper insertion for long routes
items.node_era_note: At 28nm gate oxide robust, antenna fixed with jumpers; at 7nm-and-below thin oxide and high M1-M3 density needs diode insertion during route and early antenna checks

items.symptom: detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Break down DRC by type: spacing, EOL, via enclosure, cut spacing, min step
first_checks.why_first: cheapest to identify rule family causing hotspot

first_checks.check: Check detail router options: via ladder, via optimization, taper length, wrong-way jog allowance
first_checks.why_first: rules out setting mismatch before blaming design

first_checks.check: Check cell edge and PG strap proximity of markers: within 1-2 tracks of cell boundary or strap
first_checks.why_first: identifies cell abutment vs pure routing

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If DRCs disappear when disabling via ladder / stacked via optimization, vs persist even with single-cut vias only
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: via enclosure / stacked via / cut spacing rule if disappears without ladder
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: pin access / M1 spacing if persists with single-cut only

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If markers cluster at stdcell boundary or at PG strap edge with 0.5 track alignment, vs spread random in channel center
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: cell edge spacing / double-patterning color conflict at boundary if at edge
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: non-default rule / wide-wire spacing if random in channel

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun detail route with relaxed taper and allow off-track jogs: if fix rate >70%, access related
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: pin access / taper length / off-track access issue if relaxed jog fixes
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: DRC deck vs router rule mismatch if still fails relaxed

common_root_causes.cause: Pin access failure: M1-V1 spacing, cell pin enclosure, via1 over pin
Via enclosure, stacked via, or cut spacing rule violation from via ladder optimization
Non-default rule / wide wire / shielding spacing not honored by global router
Cell abutment / double patterning odd cycle / color spacing at cell edge
Detail router rule deck vs signoff DRC deck mismatch (e.g., EOL, min step)

items.classic_trap: Blaming global router overflow when root is detail rule deck mismatch or via ladder rule that global router never sees
items.node_era_note: At 28nm global clean usually meant detail clean; at 7nm-and-below detail fails even with zero global overflow due to pin access and color spacing

items.symptom: unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Plot overflow vs iteration and density vs utilization histogram across floorplan
first_checks.why_first: cheapest to see if divergence vs high but converging overflow

first_checks.check: Report macro area ratio, fence / region utilization, and narrow channel width between macros
first_checks.why_first: rules out floorplan feasibility before tuning placer

first_checks.check: Check high fanout / high pin-count nets: tie nets, scan enable, reset, and artificial high-fanout
first_checks.why_first: cheap netlist cause that blocks placement

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Lower target density by 5% and increase macro halo by 1 track: if overflow drops sharply >40% vs stays within 10% even at 60% density
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: density / macro channel too tight if sharp drop
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: netlist topology / artificial net if stays high at low density

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Remove / idealize high-fanout nets >1000 pins and tie nets: if placement converges after removal
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: high-fanout / tie-net artificial connectivity forcing long routes
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: floorplan / pin placement forcing stretch if still diverges without them

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if overflow hotspots align with IO pin entry or pin assignment side, vs centered between macros
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: IO pin placement / pin assignment forcing global route stretch if at edge
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: macro placement / fence region if centered between macros

common_root_causes.cause: High macro density with narrow channels / insufficient halo causing placement to pack
Overly high target density / utilization or ignoring routing track utilization
Bad floorplan / IO pin placement forcing long cross-chip routes
Netlist with artificial high-fanout nets (tie high/low, scan enable, reset) not buffered
Fence / region constraints / color / voltage area fragmentation leaving unusable pockets

items.classic_trap: Running more global placement iterations expecting convergence when floorplan is fundamentally unroutable due to macro density
items.node_era_note: At 28nm unroutable placement usually high cell density >80%; at 7nm-and-below unroutable at 60% due to pin density and M0 congestion even with low cell density

items.symptom: Congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: View layer-by-layer congestion heatmap (not just overall density map)
first_checks.why_first: overall density can look fine while a single metal layer is critically oversubscribed in a narrow region

first_checks.check: Check the congestion map against macro boundaries and high-pin-count cells in the hotspot region
first_checks.why_first: macro abutment zones and dense pin arrays are the single most common hidden congestion source behind clean-looking density

first_checks.check: Run the global router's congestion report (per-gcell overflow counts by layer) before looking at DRCs
first_checks.why_first: distinguishes genuine capacity problems from detailed-router path-finding failures, which have completely different fixes

first_checks.check: Check if hotspot region uses double-via or ECO cell insertions that consumed routing tracks
first_checks.why_first: post-ECO track starvation is a frequent late-stage surprise that looks like congestion but has a different fix

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Halve cell density in the hotspot gcell region via placement blockage and re-run global route
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if global-route overflow disappears, the congestion was genuine density-related and you need local cell spreading or halos
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if overflow persists, the issue is macro pin access or layer-direction conflict, not cell density

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Flip the preferred routing direction of the offending metal layer in the hotspot region only and re-run global route
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if overflow clears, you had a layer-direction conflict (typically near rotated macros or cross-boundary routes)
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if overflow persists, direction was not the cause

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Route the hotspot region with cell-level pin-access (patch) turned off to see if pin-access alone creates the overflow
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if overflow disappears, the issue is pin-access geometry consuming routing resources, not net congestion
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if overflow persists, it is genuine net congestion

common_root_causes.cause: Macro adjacency: two large macros with complex pin interfaces placed too close, consuming all lower-metal routing resources in the channel
Huge netlist fanout nets (clock gating, resets, test) creating local routing demand spikes on a single metal layer
Standard-cell placement ignoring metal-layer direction constraints, creating layer-direction conflicts
Post-ECO routing track starvation from double-via insertion or ECO cell density

items.classic_trap: Engineers add halos or spread cells everywhere instead of checking per-layer congestion, which fixes nothing when the actual cause is a macro pin-access or layer-direction problem on a single metal layer.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, lower metal pitches mean macro pin-access congestion is far worse and appears at much smaller inter-macro gaps than at 28nm.

items.symptom: Setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Check if violations are on paths sharing a single clock domain with excessive insertion delay or skew
first_checks.why_first: CTS-induced setup violations localized to one clock domain point to clock-tree structure problems, which are cheaper to fix than redesigning data paths

first_checks.check: Verify that clock latency is within the SDC target for each clock domain (compare post-CTS timing with post-placement pre-CTS timing)
first_checks.why_first: a jump in violations coinciding with CTS means clock insertion delay ate into setup slack, which is a different root cause than data-path issues

first_checks.check: Report whether the violations cluster near macro boundaries or in specific physical regions
first_checks.why_first: spatial clustering suggests placement or floorplan issues rather than logic or constraint problems

first_checks.check: Check for clock-gating cells with high output capacitance that the CTS engine struggles to buffer
first_checks.why_first: unusual clock-gate structures can silently create large insertion delays in one subtree

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run timing with the clock tree back-annotated to post-CTS parasitics but data-path still at placement-estimated parasitics
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if violations appear mainly on paths where clock latency increased, the CTS is the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if violations existed before CTS with similar slack, the issue was already in the data path and CTS just exposed it

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check timing on the same failing paths with an ideal clock network (set_ideal_network on the clock root)
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if violations vanish, the clock tree insertion delay or skew is the culprit, not the data path
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if violations remain, the data path itself is too slow regardless of clock quality

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Isolate whether all failing paths share one clock subtree root (same clock buffer chain) versus spread across unrelated subtrees
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if they share one subtree root, a local CTS structural issue (bad pin, wrong NDR, congestion blocking buffer insertion) is likely
