discriminating_experiments.rules_out: uniform density problem

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check the experiment using the actual congestion analysis versus a placer-estimated density
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: true congestion; need adjustment
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: false alarm from placer's density estimate

common_root_causes.cause: Macro or IP placement blocks region and causes re-routing around it
High-fanout net (clock/reset/scan) topology creating hot spots
Layer assignment or track utilization mismatch (e.g., too many pins on lower metal)
Cell row utilization reporting was misleading; global route finds true hot spots
Wrong routing blockage layer setting in the flow

items.classic_trap: Trusting the placer's reported utilization as a true picture of the placed design without checking the actual routing congestion heatmap.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, the routable area is dominated by pin accessibility and track pattern, so pin density > cell density often dominates congestion.

items.symptom: setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Look at skew report and whether clock latency targets are met on the failing paths
first_checks.why_first: rules out clock skew as the cause in seconds

first_checks.check: Check whether the failing paths cluster around specific clock-gating cells or the CTS tap point
first_checks.why_first: rules out clock-tree-architecture issues

first_checks.check: Check whether CTS was done with a netlist that includes all clock cells and is consistent with the post-CTS netlist
first_checks.why_first: rules out the common 'clock cells missing in CTS view' mistake

first_checks.check: Look at the cell delay transition time (slew) on the launching/capturing clock pins
first_checks.why_first: rules out clock-buffer slew degradation masquerading as setup

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If failing paths share one or a few clock-gating cells with high insertion delay, it's skew/latency root cause; if they spread across hierarchies, check transition times or netlist issues
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: skew/latency imbalance causing the failure
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global transition or netlist issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If launch/capture skew is large only on the failing paths, run skew-opt with finer granularity or balance skew across more levels
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: skew-tuning needed
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: uneven buffer strength needed

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Look at the path with timing path mode single-clock vs inter-clock
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: inter-clock path issue (unrelated clocks)
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: single-clock balance issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check whether CTS treated the failing clock as a leaf or propagated its own delay target
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: CTS target setting wrong
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: actual physical issue

common_root_causes.cause: Excessive clock skew from unbalanced clock tree
Clock-gating cells with high latency and skewed taps
Clock tree doesn't include some clock cells (set_clock_groups or clock-view mismatch)
Transition time degradation on long clock lines or large cells driving clock pins
Operating condition or analysis view mismatch (e.g., worst-case vs typical, multi-mode analysis missing)

items.classic_trap: Treating setup violations as a data-path problem (re-sizing cells) when the actual cause is clock skew from gating/CTS architecture.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, clock tree resistance matters much more and clock-buffer-only fix doesn't suffice; need to balance drive strength and wire length.

items.symptom: hold (min-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Check whether the failing paths share a common clock-pinning cell or skew group
first_checks.why_first: rules out skewed clock root cause in seconds

first_checks.check: Run skew-opt for hold only (a hold fix) and see if violations are easily resolvable
first_checks.why_first: rules in/out whether it's an 'easy hold' or a deeper issue

first_checks.check: Check the data-path for high-drive buffers and short data delays on the failing paths
first_checks.why_first: rules out 'too-fast data' common cause

first_checks.check: Look at the scan chain / DFT mode in which holds are reported and verify the mode is realistic
first_checks.why_first: rules out a mode-mismatch root cause

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If all failing paths originate at the same clock-launch point with short data delay, it's skewed clock; if they span random origins, it's data path
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: clock skew root cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: data-path root cause

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run hold-fixing with only delay-cell insertion and observe whether the violation magnitude matches expected delay
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: fixable with simple delay padding
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: deeper clock-tree issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare across analysis modes (functional vs scan) to see whether violations appear in both

items.classic_trap: blindly inserting hold buffers until the report is clean while creating new hold or setup problems elsewhere
items.node_era_note: advanced nodes need more hold corners and variation-aware skew margins than 28nm

items.symptom: IR-drop-induced timing failure

first_checks.check: Overlay failing timing endpoints on static and dynamic IR-drop maps for the same scenario
first_checks.why_first: spatial correlation is the cheapest confirmation that supply droop matters

first_checks.check: Check power-net connectivity, missing straps/rings/vias, and supply setpoints in the failing region
first_checks.why_first: gross power-delivery opens explain large local drop quickly

first_checks.check: Review activity vectors, clock enable, and simultaneous switching assumptions used for IR analysis
first_checks.why_first: dynamic droop failures can appear only under specific high-current windows

first_checks.check: Compare timing slack with nominal supply versus annotated supply voltage
first_checks.why_first: quantifies how much slack loss is directly due to IR annotation

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun timing with IR-drop annotation disabled or with nominal voltage and compare failing paths
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: IR-drop-caused timing if the same endpoints clear or gain significant slack
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: IR-drop cause is excluded if slack and failing endpoints are essentially unchanged

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Reduce activity or gate clocks in the suspect region and rerun dynamic IR and timing
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: dynamic current spike if local droop and failures drop sharply
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: dynamic spike is excluded if droop and failures persist under reduced activity

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Add local decap or strengthen a nearby power strap in a trial floorplan/power mesh and reanalyze
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: local power-delivery deficit if local IR and timing improve
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: local power-delivery deficit is excluded if IR map changes little and failures remain

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run the same timing at a higher voltage corner with similar constraints
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: voltage-margin-sensitive IR if failures disappear at higher voltage
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: IR margin sensitivity is excluded if failures persist with similar slack loss

common_root_causes.cause: insufficient local power mesh or decap near high-current logic
dynamic current spike from simultaneous clock/data activity
missing or broken power via/strap connection
overly optimistic activity/vector set for IR analysis
power-domain crossing or isolation cell supply modeling error

items.classic_trap: debugging timing constraints path-by-path while all failing endpoints sit in one supply-droop neighborhood
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below has tighter voltage margins and more dynamic-IR sensitivity than 28nm

items.symptom: clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: Sort failing sinks by insertion delay error, clock branch, buffer depth, and distance from root
first_checks.why_first: shows whether divergence is branch-local or global

first_checks.check: Verify clock latency/skew targets, max transition/cap, and useful-skew allowances
first_checks.why_first: unachievable targets are a common non-physical cause

first_checks.check: Inspect routing blockages, macro corridors, NDRs, and pin access along failing clock branches
first_checks.why_first: physical detours are a direct cause of late sinks

first_checks.check: Check clock buffer load/fanout and whether oversized/undersized buffers were chosen
first_checks.why_first: load-driven delay is cheap to spot in the clock report

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun CTS with relaxed max transition/cap and relaxed skew targets while keeping floorplan fixed
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: over-constrained targets if most sinks then meet insertion delay
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: over-constrained targets are excluded if sinks still diverge similarly

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily remove clock-routing blockages or allow additional layers for clock trial
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: blockage/detour congestion if insertion-delay spread collapses
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: blockage/detour congestion is excluded if the same branches still miss targets

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rebuild only the failing clock branches while freezing the clock root and good branches
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: local branch topology/load issue if rebuilt branches meet targets
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: local branch issue is excluded if global root/source mismatch remains across branches

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Plot insertion delay versus Manhattan distance for sinks
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: routing detour/blockage if delay grows sharply with distance in specific corridors
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: detour problem is excluded if delay error is scattered independent of distance

common_root_causes.cause: insertion-delay/skew targets too aggressive for floorplan and library
clock branch detours around macros, blockages, or routing restrictions
overloaded clock buffers or unbalanced fanout
poor root location or topology choice
library/buffer delay model mismatch with CTS assumptions

items.classic_trap: tuning skew targets repeatedly while ignoring that floorplan obstacles make the target physically unreachable
items.node_era_note: advanced nodes have stricter clock NDRs and variation, so insertion-delay spread is harder to close than at 28nm

items.symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: Find the first divergence point in the connectivity comparison and identify the mismatched net/port boundary
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to separate netlist, layout, and extraction boundary issues

first_checks.check: Verify netlist and layout versions, ECO history, and whether the compared sources are synchronized
first_checks.why_first: version mismatch is extremely common and cheap to rule out

first_checks.check: Inspect physical shapes, pins, vias/cuts, and abutment around the mismatched net
first_checks.why_first: real opens/shorts are confirmed visually at the first mismatch

first_checks.check: Review extraction options for short resolution, power/ground recognition, and floating shapes
first_checks.why_first: extraction settings can falsely merge or drop nets

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Extract with short-detection sensitivity relaxed or with specific net merging disabled and rerun LVS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: extraction-rule false short if the reported short disappears
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: extraction-rule false short is excluded if the same short remains

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Manually trace/connect the suspect net in a small layout window and re-extract
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: real open or missing via if connectivity follows the corrected shapes
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: real open is excluded if mismatch remains despite correct visible connectivity

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare against the previous known-good layout/netlist pair
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: late ECO/version mismatch if mismatch appears only after the recent change
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: recent change is excluded if the same mismatch existed before the change

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run a small-window connectivity extraction with pin/via recognition debug enabled
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: pin/via recognition issue if shapes are connected but the net remains open
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: recognition issue is excluded if the shapes are visibly disconnected or missing

common_root_causes.cause: netlist/layout version mismatch after ECO
missing via/cut or open contact causing an open net
accidental metal overlap or spacing violation causing a short
extraction rule/options misconfiguration
port/pin name or boundary mismatch between blocks

items.classic_trap: assuming the extractor is wrong before checking version sync and the actual shapes at the first mismatch
items.node_era_note: below 28nm, cut/via rules and multi-patterning make real opens/shorts and extraction sensitivity more likely

items.symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: Inspect the first mismatched device instance and compare drawn geometry with netlist parameters
first_checks.why_first: directly shows whether the mismatch is physical or parameter interpretation

first_checks.check: Check device parameter extraction: W, L, fingers, multipliers, and parallel devices
first_checks.why_first: size mismatches often come from equivalent but differently represented parameters

first_checks.check: Verify whether dummy devices, fill transistors, well taps, or guard-ring devices are being extracted
first_checks.why_first: extra devices are commonly non-functional extraction artifacts

first_checks.check: Compare PDK library definitions and LVS rule deck device classes for both sources
first_checks.why_first: device class or property mapping errors cause systematic size/extra-device mismatches

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Dump extracted device parameters for one mismatched instance from layout and netlist sides
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: parameter equivalence issue if W/L/fingers/multipliers differ only by folding or parallel representation
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: parameter equivalence issue is excluded if the drawn device geometry itself differs from the netlist intent

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Disable extraction of dummy/fill/tap devices or tag them as non-electrical and rerun LVS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: dummy/fill recognition if extra devices disappear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: dummy/fill recognition is excluded if extra devices remain and are electrically connected

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Regenerate the netlist from the latest schematic and rerun against unchanged layout
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: stale netlist/ECO mismatch if mismatches clear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: stale netlist is excluded if mismatches persist with a fresh netlist

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run the same layout through another rule deck or PDK version
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: rule deck/device definition issue if only one deck reports mismatches
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: rule deck issue is excluded if all decks report the same device mismatches

common_root_causes.cause: stale netlist or unpropagated ECO
dummy/fill/guard devices extracted but absent from netlist
device multiplier/finger/parallel parameter interpretation mismatch
PDK or rule-deck device class/property mapping error
manual layout edit changing device geometry

items.classic_trap: treating every extra extracted device as a real circuit transistor instead of checking dummy/fill/tap extraction
items.node_era_note: advanced nodes have more required dummy/fill and device-array rules, so extra-device LVS noise is more common than at 28nm

items.symptom: antenna (process-antenna-effect) violations at signoff

first_checks.check: Group antenna violations by net, layer, and connected gate count
first_checks.why_first: antenna is ratio-based, so clustering identifies systematic routing or rule issues

first_checks.check: Check antenna rule calculation mode, layer-specific limits, and signoff options
first_checks.why_first: wrong calculation mode can create broad false failures

first_checks.check: Identify long routes on lower metal layers feeding small gates
first_checks.why_first: that pattern is the classic physical antenna cause

first_checks.check: Review jumper, layer-hop, and diode insertion strategy for failing nets
first_checks.why_first: fix strategy availability determines whether violations are design or flow gaps

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun antenna signoff with alternate calculation mode or temporary rule relaxation
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: rule/signoff-setup issue if most violations disappear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: rule/signoff-setup issue is excluded if the same nets fail under reasonable rule modes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Insert layer jumpers or reroute a sample of failing nets to higher metal and recheck
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: route-layer antenna collection if sample violations clear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: route-layer collection is excluded if violations persist despite legal layer hops

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Add protection diodes or enable diode insertion on a sample of failing gates and recheck
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: gate protection deficit if diode insertion clears violations
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: gate protection deficit is excluded if violations remain after diodes are legal and connected

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare antenna report before and after late routing ECOs
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: late ECO routing if new violations trace to recently changed nets
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: late ECO cause is excluded if violations existed before the ECOs

common_root_causes.cause: long lower-metal routes collecting charge on small gates
missing jumpers or layer hops in routing strategy
high-fanout nets with large metal-to-gate area ratios
antenna signoff rules or calculation mode set too strictly
late ECO routes creating new antenna patterns

items.classic_trap: treating antenna violations like ordinary spacing DRCs and clearing metal without fixing the collected charge/gate ratio
items.node_era_note: advanced nodes with thinner oxides and stricter antenna limits need more jumpers/diodes than 28nm

items.symptom: detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Map hotspots to pins, vias/cuts, blockages, NDRs, and layer boundaries
first_checks.why_first: detailed DRCs usually originate at access and rule boundaries, not global capacity

first_checks.check: Check local track utilization and layer-specific demand at the hotspot grids
first_checks.why_first: global routing can miss layer-local track exhaustion

first_checks.check: Review via/cut spacing, end-of-line, min-area, and patterning/coloring constraints
first_checks.why_first: advanced rules create hotspots even with enough nominal tracks

first_checks.check: Inspect pin shapes, pin layers, and allowed access directions
first_checks.why_first: pin access choices often dictate detailed-route legality

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun detailed routing with additional pin-access layers/directions or slightly enlarged legal pin shapes
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: pin-access bottleneck if hotspot DRCs clear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: pin-access bottleneck is excluded if DRCs remain with more access freedom

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily relax one suspected rule class, such as via/cut spacing or NDR shielding, in a trial run
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: rule-specific bottleneck if that hotspot class disappears
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: rule-specific bottleneck is excluded if hotspots remain despite the relaxed rule

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rip up and reroute only hotspot nets with different layer bias or spacing
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: local net interaction if only those nets clear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: local net interaction is excluded if DRCs shift to adjacent nets, indicating shared capacity

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare global-routing congestion estimate with detailed DRC locations at the same grids
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: global-underestimation/pin-access modeling gap if global is clean but detailed DRCs cluster at pins
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global-underestimation is excluded if both global estimate and detailed DRCs show the same congestion

common_root_causes.cause: pin-access or via/cut rule conflicts
local track exhaustion near macros, pins, or blockages
advanced patterning/coloring or spacing rules
global routing resource model underestimating detailed-route demand
NDR/shielding constraints consuming local routing resources

items.classic_trap: assuming clean global routing means no congestion and rerunning detailed routing without changing access, rules, or layer bias
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, detailed DRCs are often cut/coloring/pattern-rule driven rather than simple metal-spacing driven as at 28nm

items.symptom: unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Check fine-grid placement density and overflow by region, not just total utilization
first_checks.why_first: local density above legal capacity is the most direct placer divergence cause

first_checks.check: Audit macro locations, halos, keepouts, placement blockages, and well/tap rule areas
first_checks.why_first: unusable reserved area can make legal placement impossible even at moderate total density

first_checks.check: Review cell inflation factors from congestion, timing, or useful-skew optimization
first_checks.why_first: inflation can silently turn a legal density into an unroutable one

first_checks.check: Inspect fixed pins, IO/IP boundaries, and channel widths between macros
first_checks.why_first: narrow corridors are common sources of overflow and routing failure

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Lower the placement density target or allow temporary overflow in a trial global placement
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: density/inflation pressure if placement converges at lower target
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: density pressure is excluded if it still diverges with ample nominal slack

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Relax or shrink macro halos/keepouts in a trial floorplan and rerun placement
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: halo/keepout over-reservation if overflow clears
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: halo/keepout over-reservation is excluded if overflow remains in the same regions

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Freeze macros and disable timing-driven inflation/useful skew, then place standard cells only
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: macro/floorplan bottleneck if standard cells place cleanly with macros moved or constraints relaxed
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: macro/floorplan bottleneck is excluded if standard cells still overflow with realistic fixed macros

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run global placement with routing-resource demand deflated or routing congestion optimization disabled
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: over-aggressive congestion/timing objectives if placement converges
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: congestion objective issue is excluded if placement still overflows with deflated demand

common_root_causes.cause: local placement density exceeding legal capacity
macro halos/keepouts/blockages removing usable area
poor macro placement creating narrow channels
over-aggressive cell inflation for congestion or timing
insufficient routing layers/tracks for the net demand in advanced nodes

items.classic_trap: iterating placer/router options while the floorplan still contains a local density or macro-corridor impossibility
items.node_era_note: below 28nm, lower usable density targets and more well/tap/coloring keepouts make placement overflow appear earlier

items.symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Global route congestion map (overflow histogram) overlaid on layout
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to localize hotspots beyond what density alone shows

first_checks.check: Pin density / pin access map in the same hotspot regions
first_checks.why_first: local pin clustering often drives congestion even when overall density is fine

first_checks.check: Macro/blockage placement and channel widths near hotspots
first_checks.why_first: cheap visual check for pinched routing channels between macros

first_checks.check: Layer-by-layer routing utilization near hotspot
first_checks.why_first: identifies whether congestion is layer-specific (e.g., one metal layer starved)

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run global placement with higher target density / more whitespace only in hotspot region
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: congestion drops substantially -> true placement-driven congestion
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: congestion persists -> points to structural (pin/macro) cause, not density

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if hotspot correlates with a specific macro's pin edge or hard IP boundary
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: hotspot hugs macro boundary -> macro pin access is root cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: hotspot is diffuse across standard-cell area -> not macro-driven

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare congestion map before/after adding routing blockages or halo around macros
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: adding halo relieves congestion -> confirms macro-adjacent routing squeeze
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no change -> macro not the cause

common_root_causes.cause: local pin/cell clustering (e.g., dense mux or bus fanout)
macro placement leaving narrow routing channels
insufficient routing blockage/halo tuning around hard IP
global placement not congestion-aware enough (bad cost function tuning)
over-constrained layer usage (e.g., too many nets forced to lower layers)

items.classic_trap: Assuming overall placement density is the culprit and globally spreading cells, which wastes area/timing without fixing a localized pin-access or macro-channel problem.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, via pillar and multi-patterning restrictions make even moderate congestion much harder to resolve than at 28nm, so hotspots that were fixable by ECO at 28nm may require re-placement at advanced nodes

items.symptom: setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Compare pre-CTS (ideal clock) vs post-CTS timing on the same paths
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to see how much of the violation is clock-latency-induced vs pre-existing

first_checks.check: Check clock insertion delay and skew on the failing path's launch/capture pins
first_checks.why_first: directly shows if CTS introduced adverse skew

first_checks.check: Check for useful-skew opportunities already consumed or CTS target mismatches
first_checks.why_first: quick check on whether skew scheduling was applied as intended

first_checks.check: Physical location/routing detour of the failing data path post-CTS buffering
first_checks.why_first: CTS buffer insertion can push data-path cells or add routing detours

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-time the path with post-CTS actual clock latencies but zero skew (idealized) applied manually
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violation disappears -> skew/latency from CTS is the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violation remains -> underlying data path is the bottleneck, not CTS

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if failing endpoints cluster around specific clock-tree branch/leaf regions
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: clustering around one branch -> local CTS imbalance
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: failures spread randomly across the design -> more likely global data-path or library/timing-derate issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare setup slack at same corner pre- and post-clock-tree optimization (CTS opt) step
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: large slack recovery after CTS-opt indicates skew scheduling not yet converged
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no change indicates true logic/interconnect delay problem

common_root_causes.cause: clock skew/latency changes from real (non-ideal) clock tree vs ideal clock used during placement
long/high-fanout data paths with insufficient buffering
routing detours introduced by CTS buffer placement obstructing data nets
overly pessimistic OCV/derate applied uniformly post-CTS
useful skew not yet exploited by the CTS engine

items.classic_trap: Blaming 'CTS made it worse' and re-running clock tree synthesis repeatedly, when the real issue is a marginal data path that was always going to fail once ideal-clock optimism was removed.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, useful-skew based CTS optimization is much more aggressively used to close setup than at 28nm, where designers more often just fix the data path instead

items.symptom: hold (min-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Check whether violations are widespread (many short paths) vs isolated to specific register clusters
first_checks.why_first: cheap categorization that quickly narrows between global CTS/skew issue vs local path issue

first_checks.check: Clock skew between launch and capture flops on failing paths
first_checks.why_first: hold violations are extremely sensitive to skew, so this is the first physical suspect

first_checks.check: Check if violating paths are between different clock domains or clock-gating boundaries
first_checks.why_first: cheap structural check since domain crossings are classic hold-violation sources

first_checks.check: Review hold-fixing buffer insertion history/logs from the tool
first_checks.why_first: reveals whether hold-fix cells were already attempted and exhausted in that region

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Set clock skew to zero (ideal) for the failing launch/capture pair and re-check hold
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violation persists at zero skew -> genuine min-delay/data-path issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violation disappears -> skew is the true cause, driven by CTS

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if failing paths all cross the same clock-gate/ICG cell or same clock-tree branch merge point
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: common branch/ICG confirmed -> local CTS structural imbalance
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no common structure -> distributed root cause, likely data-path or library issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare hold slack at fast (min) corner with and without on-chip variation derating for clock paths
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: hold recovers substantially without derate -> excessive clock-path pessimism is inflating the violation
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no change -> not a derating artifact

common_root_causes.cause: clock skew between launch/capture flops introduced by real clock tree
short/fast data paths (e.g., adjacent flops with minimal logic)
clock domain crossing or divider/gating boundary mismatch
excessive OCV/derate pessimism on clock paths vs data paths
hold buffers inserted but themselves subject to variation causing residual violations

items.classic_trap: Blindly inserting delay/hold buffers everywhere a violation shows up without checking for a common skew source, causing area/power bloat and sometimes creating new setup risk.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, hold fixing is far more painful because buffer delay is smaller relative to variation, often requiring many more cells and iterations than at 28nm

items.symptom: IR-drop-induced timing failure

first_checks.check: Static/dynamic IR-drop map correlated against the failing timing paths' locations
first_checks.why_first: directly connects the two before deeper analysis

first_checks.check: Power grid density (strap/via count) in the failing region vs rest of chip
first_checks.why_first: cheap visual/structural check for thin power mesh areas

first_checks.check: Switching activity / toggle rate of nearby high-activity logic (e.g., clock buffers, high-fanout drivers)
first_checks.why_first: identifies local current demand spikes causing localized drop

first_checks.check: Decap placement density in the hotspot region
first_checks.why_first: cheap check for missing local charge buffering

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run timing signoff with a flat/derated voltage (no location-based IR-drop map) vs with the IR-drop-aware voltage map
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violations appear only with IR-aware analysis -> confirms IR-drop is the driver, not pure delay
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations exist even with flat voltage -> underlying timing margin issue independent of IR

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if failing cells sit specifically on weak power-grid nodes identified in the drop map
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: spatial correlation strong -> power grid weakness confirmed as cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: failing cells are on well-strapped nodes -> IR-drop unlikely to be the driver

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Simulate with reduced local switching activity (vector-based dynamic IR) vs vectorless estimate
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: dynamic (vector-based) shows much worse local drop than vectorless -> activity-driven, not static grid weakness
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: similar in both -> static grid design is the bottleneck, not activity pattern

common_root_causes.cause: thin/insufficient power straps or via density in a local region
localized high switching activity (clock buffers, high-fanout nets) not accounted for in static analysis
insufficient decoupling capacitance near hotspot
package/C4 bump placement causing localized supply starvation
vectorless IR analysis assumptions too optimistic vs real vector-based activity

items.classic_trap: Treating it as a pure timing/library issue and adding buffers or upsizing cells, which increases current draw and can worsen the IR drop instead of fixing it.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, IR-drop signoff is far more central to timing closure and often requires co-optimization with power grid design from the start, unlike 28nm where it's often a late-stage check

items.symptom: clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: CTS log/report for convergence status and target vs achieved insertion delay per sink group
first_checks.why_first: cheapest direct read of what the tool itself reports as unmet

first_checks.check: Physical distribution of the divergent sinks (clustered vs scattered)
first_checks.why_first: quickly separates a local physical obstruction from a global spec/constraint problem

first_checks.check: Check clock tree exception/constraint file for conflicting skew groups or non-default rules
first_checks.why_first: cheap check for constraint authoring errors before blaming the physical design

first_checks.check: Buffer/inverter library availability and drive-strength options used by CTS in the divergent region
first_checks.why_first: confirms whether the tool had adequate cells to hit the target

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Relax the insertion-delay/skew target for the divergent sinks and re-run CTS locally
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: convergence achieved easily -> original target was too aggressive for that region's physical constraints
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: still fails even relaxed -> real physical obstruction/blockage issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check routing congestion or blockages specifically along the clock-tree route to the divergent sinks
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: heavy blockage/congestion found on the route -> physical obstruction is the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: route is clear -> points to constraint/library issue instead

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare divergent sinks against clock-domain or skew-group boundary definitions
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: divergent sinks all sit at a domain/group boundary -> constraint grouping error
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: divergent sinks are mid-domain with no boundary nearby -> not a grouping issue

common_root_causes.cause: physical obstruction/blockage forcing long detours to reach certain sinks
overly aggressive or inconsistent skew/insertion-delay targets set in constraints
sinks physically far outlier from the bulk of the clock domain (e.g., isolated flop)
insufficient buffer drive-strength variety in the library for that region
clock-gating cell or clock-domain crossing structure not modeled correctly in CTS exceptions

items.classic_trap: Repeatedly re-running CTS with minor tweaks hoping it converges, without checking whether the divergent sinks are physical outliers that need floorplan-level intervention (e.g., moving the flop).
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, clock-tree routing resources are scarcer and skew targets tighter, so divergence is more often a true physical/resource problem than at 28nm where it's more often a constraint-authoring issue

items.symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: LVS error summary categorization (missing net vs short vs open count)
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to know which sub-type of failure to chase

first_checks.check: Check if the mismatch correlates with a recent ECO or hand-edit in the netlist/layout
first_checks.why_first: most common trigger, so checking recent changes first is cheap and high-yield

first_checks.check: Layer-vs-layer connectivity check at the flagged coordinates in the layout viewer
first_checks.why_first: directly visualizes whether metal is physically present/connected at that location

first_checks.check: Compare extracted netlist connectivity at the flagged node against schematic/RTL-derived netlist
first_checks.why_first: confirms whether the discrepancy originates in layout extraction or in the reference netlist itself

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if the same short/open appears in a clean, unmodified reference/golden layout of the same cell instance
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: does not appear in golden version -> introduced by a local edit/ECO
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: appears in golden version too -> pre-existing library/cell issue, not the edit

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Physically inspect the flagged coordinate for overlapping shapes on adjacent nets vs a genuine gap in intended connection
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: overlapping shapes from two different nets found -> true short
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no overlap, shapes just close but not touching -> false-positive from spacing/rule artifact, not a real short

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if the missing-net LVS error corresponds to a filler/tie-cell or dummy metal not intended to connect
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: net is a known non-functional (filler/tap) net -> can be waived as expected mismatch
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: net is a real signal/power net -> genuine connectivity bug

common_root_causes.cause: manual ECO or metal edit that broke or created an unintended connection
via/contact enclosure or missing via causing an open
unconnected/floating filler or tap cell flagged incorrectly
layout-vs-schematic naming/binding mismatch (pin swap or renamed net) rather than a real physical defect
extraction tool setup error (wrong layer stack or connectivity rules)

items.classic_trap: Assuming every reported short is a real physical defect and spending hours in the layout, when it's actually a naming/binding mismatch between schematic and extracted netlist.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, multi-patterning and complex via structures make opens/shorts harder to spot visually and more often require the extraction tool's own diagnostic rather than manual inspection, unlike simpler 28nm stacks

items.symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: LVS property/parameter mismatch report (W/L, finger count, multiplier)
first_checks.why_first: cheapest direct listing of exactly which parameter differs

first_checks.check: Check whether the mismatch is isolated to specific cell instances or an entire cell type across the design
first_checks.why_first: quickly separates a single bad instance from a systemic library/PDK issue

first_checks.check: Compare the library/PDK version or corner used in extraction vs the reference schematic's expected model
first_checks.why_first: common source of systematic size mismatches

first_checks.check: Check for recently added/duplicated devices (e.g., double-instantiated decap or tie cells) at the flagged location
first_checks.why_first: extra-device mismatches are often literal duplicates from automated insertion

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Extract the same cell in isolation from a clean library reference and compare device parameters
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: clean extraction matches schematic -> problem introduced downstream (during placement/edit), not in the base cell
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: clean extraction already mismatches -> library/PDK definition issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if the mismatched instances all come from one specific automated insertion step (e.g., filler, decap, or ESD insertion tool run)
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: all extra devices trace to one automated step -> tool/flow duplication bug
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: extra devices are scattered with no common origin -> more likely manual/ECO-introduced

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run extraction with a different device recognition ruleset (e.g., alternate parameter extraction rules) on the flagged instance
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: size mismatch disappears with corrected ruleset -> extraction rule/setup error
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: mismatch persists across rulesets -> genuine physical layout size discrepancy

common_root_causes.cause: stale or mismatched PDK/library version between schematic reference and extracted layout
duplicate devices from automated filler/decap/tie-cell insertion re-run
manual sizing edit in schematic not propagated to layout (or vice versa)
device recognition/extraction rule misconfiguration (wrong parameter mapping)
multi-finger device finger-count miscount due to layout generator bug

items.classic_trap: Manually resizing devices in the schematic to match the (wrong) layout extraction to silence LVS, instead of finding the actual duplication or version-skew root cause.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, finFET fin-count/finger parameters add another mismatch dimension not present in planar 28nm devices, making size-mismatch triage more complex

items.symptom: antenna (process-antenna-effect) violations at signoff

first_checks.check: Antenna violation report grouped by net and by metal layer
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to see if violations cluster on specific long nets/layers

first_checks.check: Check ratio of accumulated metal area to gate area on the flagged net
first_checks.why_first: directly identifies how far over the allowed ratio the net is, guiding fix magnitude

first_checks.check: Check if the flagged net already has diode insertion or jumper-layer routing applied
first_checks.why_first: quickly shows if a known fix mechanism just wasn't triggered/placed correctly

first_checks.check: Routing history of the net (was it routed early in a long segment on one layer before via-up)
first_checks.why_first: long single-layer runs before the transistor connects are the classic physical cause

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-route the flagged net with a layer hop (jumper) partway along its length and re-check antenna
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violation clears -> confirms classic long-wire single-layer antenna accumulation
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violation persists -> likely a different accumulation source (e.g., via stack antenna, not wire antenna)

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if violation is only at final signoff extraction but not at earlier ECO-stage antenna check
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: only appears late -> a late-stage routing/ECO change introduced it
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: present from early check too -> systemic routing pattern, not a late edit

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Insert an antenna diode on the flagged net and re-run just that net's check
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: adding diode clears violation -> confirms standard gate-oxide antenna charge issue, fixable by diode
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violation remains despite diode -> likely a via-antenna or multi-segment issue needing jumper instead

common_root_causes.cause: long single-layer wire segment routed well before connecting to the gate (classic wire antenna)
late-stage ECO routing/re-route that bypassed the antenna-aware router settings
missing or incorrectly placed antenna diode cells near the flagged pin
via-stack accumulation across many layers on a net not caught by simple wire-length heuristics
incorrect antenna rule setup/version mismatch between router and signoff tool

items.classic_trap: Blanket-inserting diodes everywhere a violation appears without checking whether a simple jumper/layer-hop would fix it more cleanly, bloating area and sometimes still missing via-stack cases.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, tighter gate-oxide margins and more routing layers make antenna violations more frequent and often require jumpers plus diodes together, unlike simpler single-fix cases common at 28nm

items.symptom: detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Detailed-route DRC violation map overlaid with global-route congestion estimate for the same region
first_checks.why_first: cheap way to see if global route simply underestimated local difficulty

first_checks.check: Specific DRC rule types flagged (spacing, min-area, min-width, via enclosure)
first_checks.why_first: different rule categories point to very different root causes

first_checks.check: Local pin access / cell orientation in the hotspot area
first_checks.why_first: pin-access-limited cells are a common cheap-to-spot cause not visible at global-route resolution

first_checks.check: Track/grid alignment and non-default-rule (NDR) net usage in the hotspot
first_checks.why_first: special routing rules can create local conflicts invisible to global routing

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run detailed routing with increased local routing effort/iterations restricted to the hotspot only
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: hotspot clears with more effort -> genuinely a router-convergence/resource issue, not a hard physical conflict
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: hotspot persists even with max effort -> real physical/pin-access constraint

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if all violations in the hotspot involve the same specific cell type or pin shape
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: one cell type dominates -> cell-level pin-access/layout issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations involve many different cell types -> more likely a general congestion/resource shortage

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare hotspot DRCs with and without NDR (wide/spaced) nets routed through the region
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: removing NDR nets clears violations -> special-rule net conflict is the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no change -> NDR nets not the driver

common_root_causes.cause: local pin-access difficulty on specific standard cells or macro pins
global route underestimating true routing difficulty (resolution mismatch)
non-default-rule (wide/spaced) nets conflicting with dense standard-cell routing nearby
insufficient detailed-router effort/iterations allotted for that region in the flow
cell orientation/flip causing pin misalignment with adjacent rows

items.classic_trap: Repeatedly re-spreading placement globally to 'fix' a hotspot that's actually caused by a handful of cells with poor pin access, wasting turnaround time without addressing the real local issue.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, pin-access DRCs dominate far more than at 28nm due to tighter design rules, so this symptom is often a placement/cell-selection issue rather than a pure router capacity issue

items.symptom: unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Overall placement utilization/density vs the target for the block
first_checks.why_first: cheapest first check for a globally over-packed design

first_checks.check: Macro floorplan review for pinwheel/blocked channels or macros placed too close together
first_checks.why_first: cheap visual check for structural floorplan problems causing global overflow

first_checks.check: Check for any nets with extremely high fanout or pathological connectivity (e.g., accidental global reset net)
first_checks.why_first: a single pathological net can blow up global placement/routing estimates cheaply diagnosed via netlist stats

first_checks.check: Placement tool log for specific divergence messages (which region/iteration it failed on)
first_checks.why_first: tool logs often point directly at the problem region before manual investigation

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Reduce target placement density/utilization significantly and re-run global placement
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: placement converges cleanly at lower density -> true over-utilization for the given floorplan
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: still diverges even at low density -> structural floorplan or netlist issue, not simple density

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Remove or isolate suspected pathological high-fanout nets and re-run placement
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: convergence achieved -> confirms pathological net was destabilizing placement
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: still diverges -> not a single-net issue, more likely floorplan/macro layout

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check placement convergence with macros fixed vs macros freely placed by the tool
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: converges when macros are manually fixed in better positions -> floorplan/macro placement was the root issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: diverges regardless of macro placement -> standard-cell-level density/netlist problem

common_root_causes.cause: overall utilization target too aggressive for the design's connectivity complexity
poor macro floorplan (blocked channels, macros too close, pinwheel arrangement)
pathological net (accidental very-high-fanout or improperly constrained net)
conflicting or over-constrained placement blockages/keepouts
tool-specific numerical instability at very high initial overflow

items.classic_trap: Cranking down utilization target repeatedly across the whole design to force convergence, masking a localized floorplan or pathological-net problem and wasting area unnecessarily.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, cell legalization is much more sensitive to local density spikes, so divergence often requires floorplan-level fixes rather than the simple global density reduction that often sufficed at 28nm

items.symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Overlay congestion heatmap with macro placement and pin boxes
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — distinguishes macro-pin-access congestion from distributed std-cell congestion

first_checks.check: Verify cell padding / keepout margins around high-pin-count macros
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — reveals whether placement blocked pin access channels

first_checks.check: Inspect layer-directive assignments on high-fanout nets (clock, reset)
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — misdirected high-fanout nets create artificial congestion

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Reroute with all macros pushed 2x farther apart; if DRCs vanish, it is macro-channel congestion
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: macro placement blocking pin access
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global routing capacity or layer-assignment issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Remove layer directives on top-10 most-congested nets; if overflow drops, it is layer-directive misassignment
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: layer directive forcing too many nets onto same layer
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: physical pin access or placement density problem

common_root_causes.cause: Macro placement creating narrow pin-access channels
Missing or insufficient cell padding on hard macros
High-fanout synthesis nets routed on upper metal without directives
Power-ring or strap blocking routing tracks at macro edges

items.classic_trap: Blaming global utilization and re-placing when the real issue is macro pin access blocked by placement or power straps
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: pin access is far tighter due to double-patterning track assignment and fewer usable tracks per layer, making macro-channel congestion much more common

items.symptom: setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Check clock insertion delay and skew on failing endpoint clocks
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — separates clock skew contribution from datapath delay

first_checks.check: Examine datapath depth and cell sizes on worst failing paths
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — reveals if paths are simply too long or undersized

first_checks.check: Verify clock-tree exceptions (float pins, exclude pins, sink type) were applied correctly
first_checks.why_first: rules out configuration error before blaming the tree

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Set all clock skews to zero in timing analysis; if violations persist, datapath is the cause, not skew
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: datapath too long or cells undersized
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: clock skew or unbalanced tree

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If all failing paths share one common clock-gating cell or clock mux, the CTS exception or structure is wrong; if they spread across unrelated hierarchies, it is local datapath
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: clock tree exception or gating structure failure
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: random datapath or placement issue

common_root_causes.cause: Clock skew pushing launch-capture relationship beyond margin
Datapath too long (placement too spread out)
Missing or wrong clock-tree exceptions on gating cells
OCV / AOCV / POCV on-clock-path variation at advanced nodes

items.classic_trap: Re-buffering the datapath when the real problem is a missing CTS exception causing large skew
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: on-chip variation (POCV) dominates setup budgets much more than at 28nm, requiring statistical timing signoff

items.symptom: hold (min-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Check clock skew on failing paths — especially launch vs capture clock insertion delay
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — hold is almost always skew-driven after CTS

first_checks.check: Identify whether failing paths are on clock-gating boundaries
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — gated-clock hold is the dominant pattern

first_checks.check: Verify hold buffers were not stripped during optimization
first_checks.why_first: rules out ECO or optimization over-aggressiveness

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Insert hold buffers only on gated-clock fanout; if violations clear, root cause is clock-gating skew
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: clock-gating induced skew
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: datapath min-delay issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If all failing endpoints share a single early-clocking region, it is placement-induced skew; if scattered, it is CTS balance failure
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: placement clustering causing early arrival
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global CTS balance problem

common_root_causes.cause: Clock skew from unbalanced gating or tree branches
Short datapaths (few logic levels) between registers
Missing hold buffers after ECO or optimization sweep

items.classic_trap: Adding delay cells on datapaths when the skew is between clock trees of launch and capture flops
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: hold is generally easier to fix due to high metal resistance creating natural delay, but clock-gating hold remains a challenge

items.symptom: IR-drop-induced timing failure

first_checks.check: Overlay dynamic IR-drop map with failing-path physical locations
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — spatial correlation confirms voltage drop causing delay

first_checks.check: Check decap placement density and power-grid stripe spacing
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — reveals grid weakness before re-simulation

first_checks.check: Inspect switching-activity vectors for peak coincident toggle windows
first_checks.why_first: rules out vector-driven worst-case vs real workload

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun timing with IR-drop annotation (voltage-aware timing); if slack matches signoff failure, IR drop is confirmed causal
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: IR drop causing cell slowdown
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: pure timing or constraint issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If failures cluster in one power domain or grid window vs scattered globally, it is local grid weakness; if global, it is system-level power delivery
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: local grid or decap insufficiency
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: package or board-level power delivery

common_root_causes.cause: Insufficient power-grid stripe density or width
High simultaneous switching on clock or data paths
Inadequate decap placement in high-activity regions
Package or board-level PDN resonance

items.classic_trap: Blaming cell delay or process variation when the path is actually slowing down due to local voltage drop
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: IR drop is drastically worse due to lower operating voltage and thinner metals, making voltage-aware timing signoff mandatory

items.symptom: clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: Check CTS exceptions: float pins, exclude pins, sink types on gating/mux cells
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — wrong exceptions cause the majority of divergence

first_checks.check: Verify placement of divergent sinks relative to clock root
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — reveals physical distance driving imbalance

first_checks.check: Inspect clock-cell sizing uniformity (no mix of drive strengths on same branch)
first_checks.why_first: rules out tool auto-sizing creating imbalance

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If all divergent sinks sit behind one clock-gating cell, fix exception on that cell; if spread across branches, re-balance tree topology
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: exception or gating-cell misconfiguration
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global tree-topology imbalance

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Force all sinks to same insertion delay target with relaxed transition; if convergence achieved, original target was physically unroutable
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: target physically impossible given placement
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: tool configuration or exception error

common_root_causes.cause: Missing or wrong CTS exceptions on clock-gating cells
Asymmetric placement of sink clusters
Mixed buffer drive strengths creating unbalanced branches
Clock-mux structure not properly balanced

items.classic_trap: Re-running CTS with more effort instead of auditing exceptions on gating/mux cells
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: useful skew methodology is more accepted, so some divergence is intentional; 28nm expected near-zero skew

items.symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: Check ECO connectivity changes vs original netlist
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — ECO disconnects cause majority of missing/shorted nets

first_checks.check: Verify power/ground pin connectivity and strap-to-pin connections
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — PG opens/shorts are common and easy to spot

first_checks.check: Inspect routing shorts in congested macro-corner regions
first_checks.why_first: rules out physical routing error before schematic blame

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run LVS with ECO netlist only (no layout changes); if mismatch persists, it is netlist-side ECO error
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: netlist/schematic mismatch from ECO
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: layout routing error

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If all shorts are between two specific nets across many locations, it is a routing DRC or via-stack error; if single location, it is local short
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: systematic routing or via-definition error
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: isolated manufacturing or extraction glitch

common_root_causes.cause: ECO introduced disconnected or wrongly connected net
Routing short in high-congestion region near macros
Power-grid strap shorting to signal routing
Extraction setup error (wrong layer mapping)

items.classic_trap: Assuming routing tool bug when the netlist ECO disconnected a pin
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: multi-patterning decomposition errors can create opens/shorts not visible in standard extraction, requiring color-aware LVS

items.symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: Check filler-cell and end-cap insertion — these appear as extra devices in layout
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — filler cells are the #1 false-extra-device report

first_checks.check: Verify tap/well-connect cell placement and recognition
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — well-tap cells often misidentified as extra transistors

first_checks.check: Compare netlist device count vs GDS device count per module
first_checks.why_first: rules out systematic sizing mismatch before spot-checking

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run LVS excluding filler and tap cells; if mismatch resolves, it is cell-recognition issue not real device error
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: filler/tap cells misinterpreted as functional devices
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: real device sizing or insertion error

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If extra devices are all minimum-size transistors in unused channel regions, they are fillers; if clustered in one functional block, it is ECO or synthesis error
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: filler or well-tap artifact
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: functional netlist error

common_root_causes.cause: Filler cells reported as extra devices
Tap/well-connect cells misidentified
ECO inserted wrong-drive-strength cell
Synthesis vs layout library cell-mapping mismatch

items.classic_trap: Debugging a 'device size mismatch' that is actually filler cells being swept into the device count
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: well-isolation and tap structures are more complex, generating more false-extra-device reports from LVS

items.symptom: antenna (process-antenna-effect) violations at signoff

first_checks.check: Check metal-layer assignment on longest violating nets
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — upper-layer long routes are the dominant antenna source

first_checks.check: Verify antenna jumper / diode insertion was enabled in routing
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — reveals if fix was never attempted

first_checks.check: Inspect gate-area ratios on violating pins
first_checks.why_first: rules out small-gate devices being disproportionately exposed

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Insert jumpers on top 10 violating nets and re-extract; if violations clear, it is pure metal-area accumulation
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: metal-area to gate-area ratio exceeded
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: diode or layer-rule misconfiguration

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If violations are all on one metal layer, it is layer-specific rule or routing preference; if across layers, it is global antenna ratio issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: layer-specific routing directive problem
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global antenna-rule or design-wide issue

common_root_causes.cause: Long uninterrupted metal routes on upper layers
Missing or disabled antenna-fix insertion during routing
Small-gate devices with large fanout
Multi-patterning decomposition creating antenna exposure on split masks

items.classic_trap: Adding jumpers everywhere instead of re-routing high-violation nets to lower layers or inserting diodes at gates
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: multi-patterning creates cumulative antenna across masks, making antenna violations much more frequent and complex

items.symptom: detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Check DRC rule deck version vs design rules used in global route
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — version mismatch causes false hotspots

first_checks.check: Inspect via-doubling and via-enclosure rules at hotspot locations
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — via rules are the most common detailed-route-only constraint

first_checks.check: Verify cell-boundary spacing and DFM rules near standard cells
first_checks.why_first: rules out cell-edge DFM constraints

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Relax via-doubling rules in test run; if hotspots vanish, it is via-rule conflict not wire congestion
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: via-rule or enclosure constraint
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: wire-spacing or track congestion

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If hotspots are all at cell boundaries vs track interiors, it is cell-level DFM; if in track interiors, it is global-route capacity overestimation
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: cell-boundary DFM or spacing rule
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global router capacity model error

common_root_causes.cause: Via-doubling or enclosure rules not modeled in global router
DFM spacing rules at cell boundaries
Global router overestimated track availability (double-patterning or coloring conflict)
Wire-spacing rules tighter than global-route grid resolution

items.classic_trap: Blaming detailed router and re-running with more effort when global router capacity model was wrong
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: DRC rule count explodes (order of 10,000+ rules), and global router almost never models all DFM rules, making hotspots routine

items.symptom: unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Check overall utilization and local utilization hot spots
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — high utilization is the primary cause

first_checks.check: Inspect macro placement and channel width between macros
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — macros blocking routing channels causes overflow even at low utilisation

first_checks.check: Verify pin-density map vs routing-track capacity
first_checks.why_first: rules out pin-congestion driving overflow

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Remove all macros and re-place; if overflow resolves, it is macro-placement blocking channels
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: macro placement blocking routing resources
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: std-cell density or netlist complexity

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Reduce utilization by 10% and re-place; if overflow resolves, it is pure capacity; if not, it is pin-density or macro-channel
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: utilization too high for available routing layers
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: structural blockage (macro or pin density)

common_root_causes.cause: Overall placement utilization too high for routing layer count
Macro placement creating unroutable channels
High pin density on specific nets exceeding track capacity
Netlist with excessive connectivity (high fanin/fanout) not partitioned

items.classic_trap: Pushing placement utilisation higher when the overflow is actually caused by macro placement blocking routing channels
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: more routing layers available but pin dimensions smaller and double-patterning reduces effective track count, so sweet spot utilisation is lower
